title: प्रथमोनुवाकः
samhita: नमो॑ अस्तु॒ नील॑ग्रीवाय सहस्रा॒क्षाय॑ मी॒ढुषे᳚ । अथो॒ ये अ॑स्य॒ सत्वा॑नो॒-ऽह-न्तेभ्यो॑-ऽकर॒न्नमः॑ ॥
pada: नमः॑ । अ॒स्तु॒ । नील॑ग्रीवा॒येति॒ नील॑ = ग्री॒वा॒य॒ । स॒ह॒स्रा॒क्षायेति॑ सहस्र = अ॒क्षाय॑ । मी॒ढुषे᳚ । अथो॒ इत्यथो᳚ । ये । अ॒स्य॒ । सत्वा॑नः । अ॒हम् । तेभ्यः॑ । अ॒क॒र॒म् । नमः॑ ॥
krama: नमो॑ अस्तु । अ॒स्तु॒ नील॑ग्रीवाय । नील॑ग्रीवाय सहस्रा॒क्षाय॑ । स॒ह॒स्रा॒क्षाय॑ मी॒ढुषे᳚ । मी॒ढुष॒ इति॑ मी॒ढुषे᳚ । अथो॒ ये । ये अ॑स्य । अ॒स्य सत्वा॑नः । सत्वा॑नो॒-ऽहम् । अ॒हन्-तेभ्यः॑ । तेभ्यो॑-ऽकरम् । अ॒क॒र॒न्नमः॑ । नम॒ इति॑ नमः॑ ॥

sayana.text: He who was called blue-throated (nilagriva) in the manner described before, he indeed becomes thousand-eyed (sahasraksha) by taking the form of Indra. Again, by taking the form of Parjanya (the rain-god), he is the pourer (midhusha), the shedder of rain. The meaning is he is the performer of the sacrifice. Salutation be to such a Rudra. And also (atho), to whichever beings are the attendants (satvanah) of this Rudra in the form of servants—to all of them I make (akaram) salutation, I bow down. (9)

bhatta_bhaskara.dhyana: "One should meditate on Shiva, with a body like the autumn moon and a cool radiance, seated on a throne along with Uma (Parvati)." (9)
bhatta_bhaskara.text:
For 'Namo astu nilagrivaya', the metre is Anushtup. The Rishi is Bhagavan Shambhu. The Deity is also Shambhu. Salutation be to the blue-throated (nilagriva), the blue-necked one. To the thousand-eyed (sahasraksha), the many-eyed one in the form of Indra. To the bountiful (midhushe)—to the shedder (of rain) through the sacrifice, or to the source of the world. Or, to the pourer of desired boons in the form of a man, by the placing of embryos. From the root 'mih' (to shed/pour). And also (atho), those who are the attendants (satvanah) of this God, his own great primary attendants (Ganas)—to them also I have made (akaram) salutation. The past tense is used in the Veda. 'Satvanah' means those who are inclined to stay (sadanashilah) near the God.

Now for the Purashcharana of this (mantra): having eaten sacrificial food (havishya) and chanting continuously for fifteen days, one completes it. Near a Shiva temple with a West-facing door, having made a fire-altar of one cubit in all directions, starting from the new moon day for ten days, and having offered a thousand Arka flowers daily, one should offer ghee and milk-porridge (payasa) to the God. Success in all matters will ensue. By this, the ritual for those desiring sons will be described. Having been initiated for five days, one should take it up in a temple of Shambhu, on a riverbank, or in a cowshed. In the temple, having invoked the God in a pot (kumbha) placed above the God or elsewhere, and having established fire to the west of it, one should offer eleven thousand Sami sticks and Sami leaves smeared with curd, honey, and ghee daily for three or five days of initiation. Daily eight thousand, or half of that, or eight hundred. One should place lotus (tamarasa) flowers on top, or leaves in their absence. Having done this, on the final day, one should feed eight thousand, or half of that, or eight hundred Brahmins. One should especially give away wealth. Having fed eleven Brahmins in the form of the eleven Rudras, and having given them some item, then to the south, in the presence of the God, having fed the Acharya more (than others), one should give him Dakshina. The Dakshina is land with seeds sown in it. The measure is also mentioned...
...

20  

...eight hundred measures with a staff, gold for earrings, and each day a quarter-Nishka should be given for making earrings. A bronze vessel for the single fire (Eka-agni) should also be given. Having done this, the one desiring a son becomes the father of a son of good nature. The lineage remains as long as the Dakshina land remains; success comes within a year. The fruit of this is connected for seven births; therefore, one should perform it.

abhinava_shankara.dhyana: Meditation on Lord Maheshvara with resplendent Goddess.
abhinava_shankara.text:
"May there be salutation to the blue-throated one (Nīlagrīva), to the thousand-eyed one (Sahasrākṣa), to the boon-granting one (Mīḍhuṣe). And likewise may I offer salutation to those attendant beings (sattvānaḥ) of his."

Having thus propitiated the solar form through the seventh and eighth [mantras], now through the ninth [mantra] one offers salutation to seek the grace of Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, who dwells on Mount Kailāsa: "Namo astu" — to Nīlagrīva, to the one of the form of the blue-throated one (Nīlakaṇṭhamūrti), may there be salutation. Of what nature [is he]? To Sahasrākṣa — the word "sahasra" (thousand) denotes the unlimited, as is known from the Smṛti: "Viśvam, śatam, sahasram ca — all these are used to mean 'all' or 'the totality'." He whose eyes are in the thousands — to him, Sahasrākṣa, meaning one of infinite, unbounded vision. By this [epithet] it is implied: "Even though you dwell on Kailāsa, my salutation here is within the field of your vision." Again, of what nature [is he]? To Mīḍhuṣe — the granter of desires to those who prostrate before him. By this [epithet], the capacity to bestow as the fruit of salutation the fulfilment of all desired objects is indicated. And by [the epithet] Nīlagrīva — meaning "one who bears the blue throat caused by drinking the Kālakūṭa poison" — the well-known glory of the Lord is implied: "The wise one takes credit for the virtue and does not become pained by the fault; he first honours it on his head and then holds the latter at the throat." By this, the Lord Supreme, who contains the entire mass of faults (like the kālakūṭa poison) within himself without allowing even a fraction to escape, yet honours every little virtue on his head, is revealed as one who is easy to worship. Having thus saluted the Blessed Lord, [the devotee] now salutes his retinue (pāriṣada): "Atho ya iti" — "And also, those sattvānaḥ (beings of virtuous nature, the close attendants)

62                    

of this Nīlakaṇṭha, those pramathaganāḥ (hosts of attendant spirits) who are of virtuous disposition and who reside in close proximity [to the Lord]" — these are indeed well-known in the Vedic texts as the divine retinue (pāriṣada) of the Blessed Lord: "Divine hosts, of many forms, eternal ones." In the Sāmaveda as well, they are described as lords of all through [the text beginning]: "Adhipatāya kṣatrapatalāya" and so forth. In the epic Bhārata also, in the worldly Parvan section: "Those who perform actions of desire, the perfected ones (siddha), the lords of the three worlds, the eternally blissful, the ever-joyful, the eloquent (vāgīśa), free from envy; those who, though possessing the eight sovereign powers (aiśvarya), are not astonished; before whom the Lord Bhava (Śiva) is perpetually present in his activities — those who have attained the auspicious union with Bhava through study, brahmacarya (celibate study), austerity (tapas), and self-restraint (dama)" — thus stated. And in the Droṇa Parvan: "His divine attendants, of various forms" and so forth — they are described as inexhaustible. In the Purāṇas also, there are well over a thousand statements concerning their greatness, and some will be cited at the point [in the later mantra] "sahasrāṇi sahasraśaḥ." Thus, "those sattvānaḥ, the pramathaganāḥ of this Lord — to them I offer salutation (namaḥ akaraṃ — I have performed namaskāra)." The seer and the deity of this mantra are the Blessed Lord himself. The metre is Triṣṭup. [The dhyāna-śloka is:] "One should meditate upon Śiva seated on a throne, of a form brilliant like the autumn moon, of cool radiance, together with Umā (his consort)." This mantra [is efficacious] for those who desire to obtain a good son. The entire procedure of purascaraṇa (preliminary ritual consecration) is to be found in the [ritual compendium called] Arṇava. Thus [ends] the ninth [mantra].

meanings.english: Salutation; obeisance; reverential bowing; surrender; homage
meanings.nirukta: Yāska (Nirukta 3.16 and 10.3) derives from √nam — 'namati praṇamati' (one bows down, prostrates). The visarga form namaḥ indicates the completed act of submission. Some nairuktikas parse as 'na + maḥ' — 'not mine', indicating relinquishment of ego, though Yāska himself favors the verbal derivation.
meanings.vedantic: In Advaita, 'namaḥ' is parsed as 'na mama' (not mine) — a surrender of kartṛtva and bhoktṛtva (doership and enjoyership). Śaṅkara in his bhāṣya treats namaḥ as complete effacement of ahaṅkāra before the Supreme. In Śaiva Siddhānta, it represents prapatti (total surrender) to Rudra-Śiva. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.22) uses 'namaḥ' in the same spirit when addressing Rudra.

panini: √नम् + असुन् (Uṇādi 4.188) → नमस् — the asun-pratyaya forms the abstract noun
P 8.3.34 — visarjanīya (ḥ) at pada-end before pause (avasāna)
P 8.3.15 — visarjanīya rules for s → ḥ in sentence-final position

lexicographical_references.nighantu: Nighantu 3.18 — listed among karmavācaka words (action-denoting terms). Naighaṇṭuka-kāṇḍa groups it with acts of reverence and worship.
lexicographical_references.amara_kosha: Amarakośa 3.3.213 — नमः listed as an avyaya (indeclinable) meaning 'praṇāma' (prostration). Amara classifies it among common liturgical expressions.

meanings.nirukta: Yāska connects dhanvan to √dhan (to produce sound) — the bow is characterized by its resonant twang when released. Also related to √dhanv (to curve/run) — its arc shape. Nirukta 9.11 notes the relationship between the bow's curve and the concept of all-pervading reach.
meanings.vedantic: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (2.2.4): 'dhanur gṛhītvā aupaniṣadaṃ mahāstram' — 'Taking up the great weapon, the bow of the Upaniṣads' — the bow is Oṃkāra (Praṇava). It is both the vehicle of destruction and liberation. In Śrī Rudram context, saluting the bow acknowledges the instrument through which divine will operates.

panini: √धन् + वनिप् (Uṇādi 4.113) → धन्वन् — vanip-pratyaya forms the n-stem noun
P 7.1.75 — an-anta (n-stem) declension paradigm: nom. धनुः (with P 8.2.7 n → anusvāra → ḥ), dat. धन्वने
P 6.4.8 — sarvanāmasthāna rules for the alternation between dhanvan-/dhanus- stems
P 8.2.7 — conversion of final n to visarjanīya in nom. sg.: dhanvans → dhanuḥ

lexicographical_references.nighantu: Nighantu 2.20 — listed among āyudha-nāmāni (weapon names). The Naighaṇṭuka tradition pairs it with iṣu as the primary weapon-set.
lexicographical_references.amara_kosha: Amarakośa 2.8.85 (Kṣatriya-varga, Āyudha) — 'dhanuḥ koḍaṇḍam' — dhanus and koḍaṇḍa are synonyms for bow. Also 'cāpaḥ śarāsanam' as further synonyms.

meanings.english: Blue-necked; blue-throated (epithet of Śiva/Rudra referring to his swallowing of the hālāhala poison)
meanings.nirukta: Bahuvrīhi: 'nīlā grīvā yasya saḥ' — one whose throat is blue/dark. The blue neck is explained by the Purāṇic narrative of Śiva swallowing the hālāhala (cosmic poison) during samudra-manthana (churning of the ocean) — his throat turned blue from holding the poison.
meanings.vedantic: The blue neck symbolizes Rudra's capacity to absorb the world's poison (suffering/evil) without being destroyed by it. In Vedānta, this represents the jñānī (knower of Brahman) who remains untouched by the world's afflictions even while present within it — like a lotus in water.

panini: P 2.2.24 — bahuvrīhi: nīla + grīvā → nīlagrīva (one whose neck is blue)
P 2.2.35 — the compound takes masculine gender matching the person described, not the final member

lexicographical_references.nighantu: Component: Nighantu 2.4 — grīvā listed among aṅga-nāmāni (body-part names). Nīla among varṇa-vācaka (color-denoting) words.
lexicographical_references.amara_kosha: Amarakośa 1.1.29 — नीलकण्ठः (nīlakaṇṭha — blue-throated) listed as one of Śiva's names. Grīvā/Kaṇṭha are synonyms: Amarakośa 2.6.92 — 'grīvā kaṇṭhaḥ' — neck synonyms.

meanings.english: Thousand-eyed; omniscient; all-seeing; one who sees everything
meanings.nirukta: Bahuvrīhi: 'sahasram akṣāṇi yasya saḥ' — one who has a thousand eyes. 'Thousand' is Vedic idiom for 'countless/infinite'. The compound signifies omniscience — the ability to see all things simultaneously.
meanings.vedantic: The thousand eyes represent sarva-jñatva (omniscience) — one of the essential attributes of Brahman (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.2). In the Puruṣa Sūkta (RV 10.90.1): 'sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt' — the cosmic Puruṣa has a thousand eyes and a thousand feet. Rudra as sahasrākṣa is identified with this cosmic Puruṣa.

panini: P 2.2.24 — bahuvrīhi: sahasra + akṣa → sahasrākṣa (one who has a thousand eyes)
P 6.1.87 — savarna-dīrgha sandhi: a + a → ā: sahasra + akṣa → sahasrākṣa

lexicographical_references.nighantu: Components: Nighantu 2.4 — akṣi/akṣa listed among netra-vācaka (eye-denoting) words.
lexicographical_references.amara_kosha: Amarakośa 1.1.42 — सहस्राक्षः listed as an epithet of Indra. In Śiva context, it indicates the omniscience shared by all supreme deities.

meanings.english: The bountiful one; the generous giver; one who rains down gifts; the munificent
meanings.nirukta: From √mih — originally 'to rain/sprinkle'. Extended meaning: 'to shower gifts'. 'Mīḍhvān = dātā' — one who gives bountifully. The perfect participle form suggests one who has abundantly given — an established giver. Sāyaṇa: 'kāmānāṃ varṣitā' — one who rains desired things.
meanings.vedantic: Rudra as mīḍhuṣa transforms from the terrifying to the bountiful — the same deity who wields arrows also showers blessings. In mantra 13, the superlative 'mīḍhuṣṭama' (O most bountiful) is the climactic address — the peak of praising Rudra's generosity.

panini: P 3.2.107 — kvasu-pratyaya (perfect participle): मिह् + क्वसु → मीढ्वस् (with cerebral ḍh per P 8.2.32)
P 5.3.55 — superlative: mīḍhuṣ + tama → mīḍhuṣṭama (most bountiful)

meanings.english: And moreover; and further; and also; furthermore
meanings.nirukta: Compound particle: atha (now/then/moreover) + u (emphatic). Introduces an additional thought — 'and furthermore'. In mantra 9: 'atho ye asya satvānaḥ' — 'and moreover, those who are his attendants'.
meanings.vedantic: Atho transitions from praising Rudra directly to acknowledging his retinue (gaṇas/attendants). This expansion from the one to the many is a hallmark of Vedic theology.

panini: P 6.1.96 — sandhi: atha + u → atho (a + u → o)

meanings.english: Who; which; what; that which (relative pronoun forming correlative clauses)
meanings.nirukta: Yāska classifies yad among relative-correlative constructions fundamental to Vedic syntax. The relative clause structure 'yā te iṣuḥ ... tayā naḥ mṛḍaya' (which arrow of yours ... by that, be gracious to us) is a defining pattern of Vedic prayer — naming the fearsome and asking for its transformation.
meanings.vedantic: The relative pronoun 'yā/yad' in Vedic prayer introduces the item of fear which the devotee then asks the deity to make auspicious. This rhetorical structure embodies surrender — not denying the terrible but asking it to become gracious.

panini: P 1.1.27 — yad is classified as a sarvanāman (pronoun)
P 7.2.102-105 — declension paradigm for yad-śabda across genders
P 8.1.36 — ya-forms can be accent-bearing or enclitic depending on position

meanings.english: This; this here; this very (proximate demonstrative pointing to something nearby)
meanings.nirukta: Idam points to what is immediate and present, contrasted with adas (remote). In mantra 7: 'imāṃ rudrāḥ' — 'these Rudras here [in all directions]'.
meanings.vedantic: The proximate 'idam' (this) vs remote 'adas' (that) establishes a spatial theology — Rudra is both 'asau' (that one yonder — the transcendent sun) and manifest 'here' (imāṃ — in all directions through the Rudras). This is the saguṇa-nirguṇa polarity.

panini: P 1.1.27 — idam classified as sarvanāman
P 7.2.108-109 — special suppletion forms: idam → imam/imām
P 7.2.85 — enad-ādeśa: idam → enam/enām (anaphoric replacement)

meanings.english: Attendants; warriors; companions; strong beings; Rudra's retinue (gaṇas)
meanings.nirukta: From sat (being/warrior) + van (possessive). 'Sattvaṃ balam yasya' — one who possesses strength/being. Sāyaṇa glosses: 'anucarāḥ' (attendants, followers). Refers to Rudra's gaṇas — the host of beings that accompany the Lord.
meanings.vedantic: In mantra 9: 'ye asya satvānaḥ' — 'those who are his attendants'. The devotee offers salutation not just to Rudra but to his entire retinue. In Śaiva theology, the gaṇas (attendants) represent the various forces and beings that serve the cosmic will of Śiva-Rudra.

panini: P 3.2.130 — vanip-pratyaya: sat + van → satvan (one who possesses being/strength)

meanings.nirukta: The emphatic first-person pronoun. In mantra 9: 'ahaṃ tebhyo'karaṃ namaḥ' — 'I made salutation to them'. The shift from plural 'we' (naḥ) to singular 'I' (aham) is significant — the individual devotee personally commits to honoring Rudra's attendants.
meanings.vedantic: In Vedānta, 'aham' is analyzed extensively — it is the locus of ahaṅkāra (ego) but also of the Ātman. 'Aham brahmāsmi' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10). Here the devotee uses 'aham' in the act of surrender — the 'I' that bows is simultaneously transcended by the act of bowing.

panini: P 7.2.86 — nominative singular suppletion: asmad → aham

meanings.nirukta: Functions as the correlative partner to yad (relative pronoun). The construction 'yā te iṣuḥ ... tayā naḥ mṛḍaya' uses yā...tayā as relative-correlative pair.
meanings.vedantic: In Vedāntic usage, 'tad' famously refers to Brahman — 'tat tvam asi' (Chāndogya 6.8.7). The correlative use here points to the identity between the terrible and the auspicious.

panini: P 1.1.27 — tad classified as sarvanāman
P 7.2.102 — declension paradigm for tad-śabda
P 7.1.25 — suppletion: nom. sg. masc. becomes saḥ (not tadaḥ)

meanings.nirukta: The most fundamental action-verb. In mantra 4: 'śivāṃ giritra tāṃ kuru' — 'O mountain-protector, make that [arrow] auspicious'. The imperative 'kuru' is a direct petition.
meanings.vedantic: The prayer 'tāṃ kuru śivām' asks Rudra to transform his arrow's nature — this is the Vedic understanding that the divine can alter the fundamental character of reality through will. In Vedāntic terms, it is asking the cosmic agent to exercise his freedom (svātantrya) benevolently.

panini: P 3.4.87 — loṭ (imperative): कृ + हि → कुरु (with special stem per P 6.1.59)
P 3.2.111 — laṅ (imperfect): अ + कृ + अम् → अकरम्
